A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SWAN optimizer research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original C4 pretraining results, optimizer ablations, gradient-distribution measurements, synthetic optimization experiments, and memory and throughput measurements.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and reports additional SWAN variants, reproduced baseline results, and experiments evaluating its new whitening approximation.

M1.justification: GradNorm changes from mean subtraction and standard-deviation normalization in v1 to uncentered RMS-style normalization in v3. Section 4.2 and Algorithm 2 also introduce Newton-Schulz with diagonal substitution (NSDS), used by SWAN‡, alongside the retained standard Newton-Schulz procedure. These alter the core gradient preprocessing.

E1.justification: C4 pretraining, quadratic and Rastrigin optimization, and simplified-transformer simulations remain. The limited coverage addition is Appendix B.2's transformer-gradient diagnostic using randomly generated token sequences, introducing a synthetic input condition beyond the retained natural-language experiments.

E2.justification: v3 Table 2 adds Apollo, Apollo-mini, and Momentum+GradWhitening to the pretraining comparisons, retaining Adam, GaLore, Low-Rank, LoRA, and ReLoRA. Momentum+GradWhitening is explicitly described as Muon-like with Nesterov acceleration disabled. These substantially expand the relevant comparator set.

E3.justification: The added SWAN† and SWAN‡ experiments enable warmup and use a global learning rate of 0.02 with scaling factor 0.05, unlike v1's principal no-warmup setting. NSDS experiments use two BF16 iterations. Throughput testing changes from four to eight A100 GPUs and adds explicit controls with and without distributed whitening computation; memory testing adds per-layer training. Consequently, throughput values are not directly comparable across versions.

E4.justification: v3 Appendix B adds condition-number and update-direction diagnostics, NSDS iteration-count sensitivity, and BF16-versus-FP32 ablations. Earlier component, learning-rate, warmup, and initialization studies remain, with synthetic optimization studies moved to Appendix I. However, v1 Figure 4's value-projection KL panel and loss-comparison panel are omitted from the retained gradient-stability experiment.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The gradient-distribution experiment retains estimation using 16 additional minibatches of size 64; its mean and standard-deviation calculations are not newly introduced statistical reporting.

E6.justification: v1's SWAN perplexities remain unchanged under SWAN-0 in v3 Table 2. Added SWAN‡ results are 30.59, 22.61, 16.63, and 13.56 across the four model sizes, under its new configuration. The reproduced 350M Adam value changes from 20.11 to 19.24. Main-table GaLore values switch to cited results, with larger-model reproductions retained in Table 6. Memory estimates also change, including 1.3B SWAN/SWAN-0 from 2.60G to 2.98G, and new throughput and NSDS-ablation outcomes are reported.

T1.justification: The GradNorm definition and Theorem 1 proof are revised to remove centering. v1's separate structured-Hessian/Newton-equivalence theorem and derivation in Appendices B.2 and H are removed; its distinct quadratic contraction theorem survives as v3 Theorem 2. The later printed RMS denominator also omits the square required by its accompanying RMS description, leaving a mathematical inconsistency.

C1.justification: The central stateless-training, Adam-level performance, and approximately 50% memory-saving claims remain. v3 adds fast whitening with Adam-like throughput without distributed gradient processing as a central contribution, and extends the memory claim through combination with LOMO. It also explicitly positions SWAN as a composition of established operators.

C2.justification: v3 adds a hypothesis connecting changed update directions to slower early but stronger late convergence, discusses noisier NSDS conditioning, and identifies operator composition and distributed scalability as unresolved issues. Conversely, it removes v1's explicit qualifications that shared Hessian diagonal blocks do not establish zero off-diagonal blocks and that practical normalization differs from the theoretical parameter grouping.

D1.justification: Appendix J substantially expands variant-specific learning rates, scaling factors, warmup, precision, and baseline tuning grids. It specifies NSDS's two iterations with beta 0.4 and distinguishes cited from reproduced comparisons. v1 already disclosed using Adam outside the selected projection weights and FP32 whitening of BF16 gradients; those are retained details, not new disclosures.

R1.justification: The expanded related-work discussion situates SWAN against Muon, Apollo, SGD-Sal, Adam-mini, PSGD, LAMB, and established gradient-orthogonalization and Kronecker-curvature methods. It more explicitly acknowledges prior uses of its components and introduces the relationship to the authors' subsequent multi-normalized gradient-descent framework.

P1.justification: The title and substantial portions of the abstract, introduction, method explanation, experimental narrative, and conclusion are rewritten. Related work moves from Section 6 to Section 2, theoretical-validation experiments move into Appendix I, appendices are reorganized, and a dedicated Open Questions and Extensions section is added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with additional memory and whitening-throughput comparisons, and the main results table gains multiple variants and baselines. New tables present memory/expressiveness, throughput, NSDS ablations, and reproduced results. Convergence and ablation plots are redesigned, while the relocated gradient-stability figure is reduced from four panels to two.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens assessment of SWAN's practical efficiency. Table 3 exposes standard whitening's throughput penalty without distributed processing and tests the NSDS remedy under controlled settings; Appendix B evaluates its numerical behavior, while broader comparisons and Appendix J improve reproducibility. These address important weaknesses in v1's broad low-overhead account and limited comparator coverage. Removed theoretical caveats and the inconsistent RMS formula are drawbacks, but the gains in experimental scrutiny, implementation guidance, and research positioning outweigh them.
